rv.q: Both the artist and the man deserve better.
House of McQueen is a triumph of form and feeling, a production that dares to match its subject’s audacity with its own.
Whether you’re a slave to fashion or, like me, a confirmed non-expert, you’ll likely find “House of McQueen” an intriguing and entertaining character study.
A theatrical dramatization of the life of Alexander McQueen has potential but House of McQueen is an imperfect attempt.
It gets the job done, but one wonders if a visionary like McQueen, who knew how to make his audience stew in discomfort, deserves something bolder.
Unfortunately, despite the first-class production, House of McQueen never quite comes to dramatic life.
"House of McQueen" feels mostly like a missed opportunity.
Saturday Church employs the tried and true trope of an alienated outsider kid finding self-acceptance and community and delivers enough zest and zip to overcome its flaws.
But this remains one of the least informative bio plays to come our way in some time.
Every scene is so short and undeveloped that the title character emerges as a jumble of clichés produced by an abusive father, an adoring mother, snobbish employers, and HIV-i...
House of McQueen is a tedious study of a remarkable individual.
Disappointingly, House of McQueen renders all that theatricality and extravagance, pain and terror, thrill and feverishness into a show that feels like a knockoff bag on Canal Street.
The play may know its subject, but doesn’t convey that knowledge effectively or dramatically.

If you go to House of McQueen – and you should – try to select seats at the center of the house, as the handrails in the aisles of the new theater are higher than usual and block the sightlines from the sides.
Split the seam of its over-the-top sensibilities, and House of McQueen offers raw humanity beneath the haute couture spectacle.
The design elements of the show itself are simply exquisite, and matched the blocking (Sam Helfrich) with a beautiful precision.
It illuminates McQueen’s chaotic personal life better than it does his iconoclastic work...

But even the charisma of Newton and the ensemble cast can’t make up for the lack of forward momentum in Sam Helfrich’s production, which feels less theatrical and daring than any of McQueen’s fashion shows.
The play, directed by Sam Helfrich, darts between eras and modes of storytelling, not really settling on a compelling through-line.
In the end, The House of McQueen fails the man it aims to honor.

But Darrah Cloud’s fever dream of a script, which is made up short scenes that jump around in time and place, is a crazy quilt of incomprehensibility that seems to lift its limited plot points from Wikipedia.

Luke Newton delivers a powerful, transcendent, cerebral performance as Alexander McQueen, which captures his conscience to the tee; moreover, he layers his emotions well and has the crowd with him every step of the way.

The show attempts to capture the fierce energy of a McQueen runway extravaganza but instead gets mired in overuse of technology, a narrative that offers little sense of time and place, and characters that don’t grow or develop across two hours (plus intermission).

cn.t: Mixed reviews for this Alexander McQueen bio-play, with critics praising its visual style and Newton's performance but finding the script shallow and episodic. The costume exhibit during intermission earns more enthusiasm than the play itself.
